newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia can be economic superpower-IMF chief.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia can be economic superpower-IMF chief.

text.p: The head of the International Monetary Fund on Thursday said a reformist Russia could become an economic superpower but the IMF would wait for government action on tax reform before freeing up more cash.
"This country can be an economic superpower but this cannot be achieved without reforms," Michel Camdessus told the budget committee of the State Duma lower house of the Russian parliament.

Camdessus said the Russian economy, struggling to achieve its first sustained growth since the fall of the Soviet Union, could grow by six percent annually and have inflation at levels of other industrial nations by the turn of the century.
But he told a news conference the IMF would not send Russia money until the government had submitted a new tax code to parliament.
Growth could occur as soon as this year but only if structural reforms were adopted, he added.
"I must tell you that the government has accepted that the transmission of the tax code to the State Duma be a prior action to the disbursement of the IMF," Camdessus said.
"They accept that we don't start paying them before they have completed this work."
The IMF has delayed several $340 million tranches of a $10 billion three-year loan because of low tax revenues.
An opinion poll released on Thursday showed most Russians wanted tax reform, Itar-Tass news agency said.
Millions of Russians have not received wages and pensions on time and Camdessus said this was one of the government's priorities, along with tax collection.

But he said he came with a message of hope and had agreed the major provisions of an economic plan for the year with Russian officials. He said talks would finish this month and he would recommend that the IMF's board approve the deal.

Camdessus said reform plans included passing the tax code, increasing central bank supervision of commercial banks and measures to "de-dollarise" the economy. By many estimates, Russians have about $20 billion in dollars hidden at home.

Official corruption would have to be curbed, the link between some large enterprises and government would have to be broken and tax debtors would have to be allowed to go broke, he said, adding: "That's life."
Camdessus said President Boris Yeltsin and a new team named in a recent cabinet shakeup were committed to reform. Yeltsin met the IMF chief on Thursday and thanked him.

"You, personally, and the experts who visit Russia on your instructions have saved us from making many mistakes in carrying out our reforms," Interfax news agency quoted the Russian president as saying.
But some Duma representatives said they wanted to amend reform plans and accused Camdessus personally of standing in the way of a better programme.
"We told Camdessus that we find it increasingly difficult to restrain people's emotions," former Soviet prime minister Nikolai Ryzhkov told reporters.
"When do you expect the fall to end?" Agrarian Party deputy Gennady Kulik asked Camdessus.
Camdessus told the deputies that Russian growth had failed to appear not because of IMF policies but because IMF recommendations had not been followed closely enough.
"You cannot ruin your own credibility by telling your people you can have a high rate of growth without reform," he told deputies in the Duma, which is dominated by conservatives.
